prompt: Styrene oxide (phenyl-substituted epoxide) opens with methanol. Under ACID, OMe ends up on the benzylic carbon; under BASE, OMe ends up on the terminal CH₂. Why does the regiochemistry flip?

options.label: Acid TS has cation character at the benzylic C (Ph-stabilized), so Nu attacks there; base is SN2-like and attacks the less hindered C.
Acid cleaves the C–O bond to the terminal C; base cleaves the C–O bond to the benzylic C — the Nu replaces whichever bond breaks.
Under acid, protonated methanol is a weak Nu that only attacks the easier primary C; under base, methoxide is strong enough to attack the hindered benzylic C.
Both pathways give the same product initially, but acid conditions equilibrate to the thermodynamically more stable benzylic ether.

explanation: Under acid, the TS has significant carbocation character — stabilized at the benzylic C by Ph. Nu attacks the C where positive character is highest. Under base, no cation; TS is SN2-like and sterics win → Nu attacks the LESS substituted CH₂. Classic regio flip, dramatically shown by styrene oxide.
